parts.latex:
Let $f(x)=3x^2+5x$.

Use the definition $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ to find the derivative of $f(x)$.

solutions.latex:
Expanding $f(x+h)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x+h)&=3(x+h)^2+5(x+h)\\ &=3x^2+6hx+3h^2+5x+5h \end{aligned}$$
so
$$\begin{aligned} f(x+h)-f(x)&=3x^2+6hx+3h^2+5x+5h-(3x^2+5x)\\ &=6xh+3h^2+5h \end{aligned}$$
Using the definition:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{6xh+3h^2+5h}{h}\\ &=\lim_{h\to0}\,(6x+3h+5) \end{aligned}$$
Apply the limit by letting $h=0$:
$$\therefore \dfrac{dy}{dx}=6x+5$$
criteria: Finds correct expression for $f(x+h)-f(x)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the definition of the derivative from first principles:

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{5(x+h)^2-3(x+h)-(5x^2-3x)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{5x^2+10xh+5h^2-3x-3h-5x^2+3x}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{10xh+5h^2-3h}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{h(10x+5h-3)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}(10x+5h-3) \\ &= 10x-3 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Differentiate $f(x)=3-x^2$ from first principles.

You may use $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.

solutions.latex:
Using the first principles definition:

$$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{\left(3-(x+h)^2\right)-\left(3-x^2\right)}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{\left(3-x^2-2xh-h^2\right)-\left(3-x^2\right)}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{-2xh-h^2}{h}\\&=\lim_{h\to 0}\left(-2x-h\right)\\&=-2x\end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ f'(x)=-2x$$
criteria: Substitutes into the first principles formula and expands correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
On a continuous function $f(x)$, $h$ is a positive number which represents the horizontal difference between two points on the function.

Which of the following would NOT give the derivative of $f(x)$?

solutions.latex:
Option A is the definition of the derivative.

Option B is the gradient of the line joining $\left(x-\dfrac{h}{2},f\left(x-\dfrac{h}{2}\right)\right)$ and $\left(x+\dfrac{h}{2},f\left(x+\dfrac{h}{2}\right)\right)$. As $h\to 0$ this gives the gradient of the tangent at $(x,f(x))$.

Option C is the gradient of the line joining $(x-h,f(x-h))$ and $(x,f(x))$. As $h\to 0$ this gives the gradient of the tangent at $(x,f(x))$.

Option D is the negative of option C, since $f(x-h)-f(x)=-\big(f(x)-f(x-h)\big)$.

So it equals $-f'(x)$, which is not the same as $f'(x)$.

Factorise the numerator and rationalise the denominator:
$$\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{x^2-2x-8}{\sqrt x-2}&=\lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{(x+2)(x-4)}{\sqrt x-2}\times\dfrac{\sqrt x+2}{\sqrt x+2}\\ &=\lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{(x+2)(x-4)(\sqrt x+2)}{x-4}\\ &=\lim_{x\to4}(x+2)(\sqrt x+2)\\ &=(4+2)(\sqrt4+2)\\ &=24\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator and denominator, then cancel the common factor $x-4$.
$$\begin{aligned} \lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{x^2-16}{8+2x-x^2} &= \lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{(x-4)(x+4)}{(x-4)(-2-x)} \\ &= \lim_{x\to4}\dfrac{x+4}{-(2+x)} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{-6} \\ &= -\dfrac{4}{3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Use the differentiation by first principles to verify that if, the gradient function of $y = 3x^2 - x$ is $y' = 6x - 1$.

solutions.latex:
Let $f(x) = 3x^2 - x$. Using first principles:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{3(x+h)^2 - (x+h) - (3x^2 - x)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{3(x^2 + 2xh + h^2) - x - h - 3x^2 + x}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{6xh + 3h^2 - h}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}\dfrac{h(6x + 3h - 1)}{h} \\ &= \lim_{h\to 0}(6x + 3h - 1) \\ &= 6x - 1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes into the first principles definition and expands, or equivalent merit
